All 110 public functions (module functions and class methods in src/verified_execution and server_mcp.py) are listed in tests/unit_inventory.json with a normal and an abnormal test. The list of public functions is computed from the source, and the listed tests are re-run under a sys.monitoring tracer that checks each declared outcome (return, raise, error value, absent result, or handled abnormal input). Every tool contract in contracts/ is in the inventory. Request violations derived from each input schema (confirmed invalid by jsonschema) are refused by the tool's validation, the shared runtime, MCP and HTTP without running anything. Replies outside each output contract's success domain are refused as INVALID_TOOL_RESULT. Durable executors no longer pass failure codes their contract does not declare (CONTRACT-FAILURE-001): IDEMPOTENCY_CONFLICT, DATABASE_BUSY and DATABASE_ERROR were added to the durable tools' contracts, and any other internal code becomes INVALID_TOOL_RESULT. A corpus of real failure scenarios stays within the declared codes.

tests/fixtures/authorization_table.json holds 108 literal grant-check rows (tool, publisher, destination, revocation, expiry) with deny reasons, and 36 end-to-end rows (grant x call) with the expected runtime, MCP and HTTP outcomes, written from the documented policy. The tests read each expectation from a row and never compute one; a mechanical check confirms that neither the test nor the table contains the condition of LocalAuthority.permits.

Two principals share one ledger. Another principal's request key, operation id, approval, MCP server or HTTP credential returns none of the first principal's data: no value, no issue number, no stored result and no replay. ExternalChangeExecutor.result now reads only the executor's own principal's operations (it returned any operation's result before).

Children are killed with SIGKILL while a real HTTP destination holds their create, before the request leaves, while holding a worker lease, and in the middle of a stream of ledger transactions. Recovery from disk alone: the held create is reconciled by lookup without a resend; the unsent one goes to human reconciliation; the lease is fenced until it expires and then quarantined, never re-dispatched; the ledger passes integrity_check and every operation's state, result and history agree.

The destination credential is sent only to the configured API host: urllib copied it onto redirects to other hosts, so redirects are now refused and returned as replies (a redirected create is a definitive rejection). Secrets in destination replies (body, fields, headers) are kept only as digests and never reach the SQLite files or the caller; argument text goes only to the approved destination; model input never reaches another destination or region; HTTP and MCP error replies do not echo request text.

docs/concurrency_inventory.json lists the thread, process, SQLite and async races. The test scans the source for concurrency primitives and fails on any site not listed (29 sites), on listed tests that do not exist, and on unchecked entries that claim tests. Seven orders are recorded as unchecked and not guaranteed, among them orders inside one SQLite transaction, multi-host storage, clock rollback and free-threaded builds.

Every transaction order of concurrent reservation (20 orders), cancellation against dispatch and result, and lease-expiry ownership switch (30 orders) is run on a fresh ledger with a controlled clock and checked against its invariants; each search finds counterexamples when one guard is removed from the ledger. Real threads and task cancellation close three paths that had no test: two callers with one external request key, the model call budget, a cancelled external call, and a stalled diagnostics reader. Orders inside one transaction are not enumerated and are recorded as unchecked.

docs/verification_scope.json separates executed from not executed for external services, official MCP and durable records. Executed items point only at evidence that ran and passed; not-executed items claim no evidence, are marked unconfirmed, list their local substitute tests and say why (for example the official conformance suite against the current source, a real rate limit, power loss, a full disk). A not-executed item that names a task keeps that task from being marked done.

HTTP is an adopted profile. The OpenAPI document served by the app now describes every response body (contracts/http_jobs.responses.json). Its paths and methods match the app's routes (the document itself is the one undocumented route); every documented status of every operation is produced by a real request and validated against its schema, and no undocumented status occurs; the documented request schema decides acceptance, except the decimal-notation rule its description announces.

Model connectors are an adopted profile. A fixture model proposes every side-effecting tool, with arguments claiming approval, while the host's side-effecting executors are live in the same process. The proposals stay inert, and even an exactly approved proposal reaches only the read-only runtime: the destination receives no request and the ledger records nothing. A control shows the same wiring does create an issue when the host calls it.

scripts/measure_operations.py measures wall and CPU time per call, peak memory, ledger bytes and cost (requests to an external service; paid API calls, always zero) for seven operations, each in its own process. The baseline was measured on main before the testing phase (07a6939); the diff of this tree against it shows no regression beyond the thresholds and identical request counts. Timings vary by machine; the tests compare only the deterministic costs exactly.

No workflow installs a proof toolchain; CI checks the recorded Lean evidence by its hashes only.

scripts/select_tests.py maps a diff to tests with config/test_selection.json. Every permission-bearing path (the launcher's pinned files, risk classes, tool contracts, destinations, limits, the runtime and adapters, workflow token permissions, the permission history) adds the 14-file safety suite, which --run names explicitly even inside a whole-suite run. Source, contract and configuration changes and any path no rule explains run the whole suite; a test file runs itself; a script or document runs the tests that name it.

scripts/verify_task.py checks one task as an independent unit: its single evidence record (validated by the same task_cases function verify_phase uses), exactly its pytest cases in a new process without a cache, each passing exactly once, and its review scope (the files bound to the record, each unchanged, changed or missing). Every done task outside the scope phase, whose 18 records predate case lists, is such a self-contained unit.

docs/dependency_sources.json is generated from the locks and the workflows: for each of the 33 runtime packages and the build backend, its exact version, artifact hash count and adoption chain (direct requirement or via another package), and every dependency install in the workflows, classified as hash-locked, a pinned tool or a diagnostic install. The tests require the record to equal what the lock and workflows say, every direct requirement of pyproject.toml to be satisfied by the lock, and the lock to name no index, path, VCS or URL source.

The dependency-vulnerabilities CI job queries OSV for the exact version of every locked package, with the standard library only, keeps the report as an artifact for 90 days and fails on any known vulnerability. CI run 45945637877 found none in the 33 packages; evidence/security/osv-scan.json is that report, transcribed from the job log, and its canonical SHA-256 equals the one the job printed. The release gate re-runs the scan and checks that the saved report covers exactly the current lock.

scripts/release_manifest.py ties one commit's tracked files (each SHA-256 and a tree digest), the hash-locked runtime and build dependencies and the built sdist and wheel (SHA-256 and size) into one manifest. The release-artifacts CI job builds with setuptools 80.9.0 installed by hash and keeps the artifacts with the manifest for 90 days; evidence/release/build-trial.json records the manifest summary of CI run 45948159854 (merge commit a6e2de9, 606 tracked files, artifacts kept 90 days).

Task and gate records are bound to the SHA-256 (or git blob id) of every file their tests checked and to their report. scripts/evidence_freshness.py classifies each record as fresh, stale or unbound and fails --require-fresh on a stale one; verify_phase --snapshot and the release decision refuse stale gates, and live runs never read old results. --refresh-gate reruns a phase in a new process and rebinds the gate, with a report of its own, only after that run passed; a failing rerun leaves the record untouched.

Each CI build is made three times from fresh copies of the tracked files: A with SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH, TZ=UTC and umask 022; B with the same epoch but TZ=Asia/Tokyo, umask 077, another path and earlier file times; C without SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH. Every differing archive member and field is recorded. In CI run 45948159854 the controlled builds A and B were not byte-identical: the wheel's file modes (external_attr, 27 members) follow the build umask, the sdist's tar and gzip times (132 members) follow file and build times although SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH was set, and 12 sdist directory modes follow the umask; without SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH the wheel's timestamps (46 members) change as well. These differences are recorded in evidence/release/build-trial.json; no reproducibility is claimed.

scripts/release_gate.py runs the static safety policy, the permission-history check, the secret audit of evidence and documentation, the saved-scan check and a live OSV scan, all of them even after a failure, and allows a release only if every one passed. The release-artifacts job needs every verification job (including the safety tests) to pass, runs the gate before building, and keeps the artifacts only on success; the gate report is always kept.

scripts/staging_trial.py runs inside one new staging directory with synthetic data only: the real MCP server over stdio with a staging ledger and a fresh environment (no host credential reaches it), the external tool against an in-memory destination, the kill switch, a backup and restore and the monitor. It refuses a host ledger outside the staging directory and leaves it untouched; the repository and the operator's home are not written. CI runs it in the locked environment.

scripts/monitor_operations.py counts operations, errors and denials per window, from the ledger (opened read-only) or from the MCP server's diagnostics, and compares the latest window with the mean of ten baseline windows: operation_spike, error_spike and error_rate (thresholds in config/monitoring.json). Steady traffic stays quiet; a burst, an error burst and a high error rate each raise their alert once per window, from both sources and from the command line (exit status 2).

scripts/audit_logs.py scans text files for credential shapes (GitHub, Stripe-like and AWS keys, bearer headers, private keys, JWTs, password or token assignments) and for the literal values of named environment variables; any finding fails with a redacted report. CI audits evidence/ and docs/, and the test also audits the real MCP server's diagnostics while it handles calls that carry a secret.

docs/permission_history.jsonl is a hash chain of permission snapshots (tool risk classes, the launcher's approved code, external destinations and their credential scope, limits, and every workflow's token permissions) with the changes between them, rebuilt from the available git history (14 entries). CI fails when the chain was edited or when the current files differ from the last snapshot; a change is recorded only with a reason and an approver.

scripts/required_checks.py runs every run step of the release verification workflow except installs, read from the workflow itself, with the interpreter of a candidate environment. The lock-candidate workflow resolves the newest allowed versions on dependency changes and weekly, installs them by hash and runs them all: run 45945589880 passed 28 of 28 required checks on the candidate set (including the 603 testing-phase cases). The candidate lock and its dependency record are kept for review.

A kill switch file revokes the grant of tools with external effects: LocalAuthority consults it before reservation, the ledger inside the dispatch transaction and the executor before any resend, so no request leaves after it is seen. It is sticky until restart and fails closed. scripts/kill_switch.py engages, reports and clears it; the repository variable VATER_EXTERNAL_TOOLS_DISABLED stops the live evidence workflow before its first request; docs/runbooks/disable_external_tools.md is the incident procedure.

scripts/backup_ledger.py takes consistent online backups with SQLite's backup API (with a manifest hash and integrity check) and restores them without overwriting a ledger. After a restore, a recorded operation is replayed, one in flight at backup time is settled by lookup and never resent, and one executed after the backup is not executed again: a restore fence stops new external dispatches until a complete destination listing shows nothing missing from the ledger, or a person reconciles it.

scripts/release_decision.py takes the required gates from the ledger (the nine initial Python phases, then the five required added-feature phases; optional phases excluded) and accepts a gate only when it is done and its evidence is executed, passed and fresh. The extended release is allowed only when every initial and added-feature gate passes, and the release job publishes the extended artifacts only on that decision. In CI run 45948159854 the decision blocked both releases, since every gate's evidence was stale at that commit, and the extended release was not published. After the gates were rebound by passing live reruns, only gate.scope.completed, whose records predate case lists, stays stale and keeps both releases blocked until a person re-verifies the scope.

All 17 operations tasks are done with executed evidence; this report reruns every mapped case in one session (151 cases). CI-only evidence: the OSV scan (run 45945637877), the lock-candidate revalidation (run 45945589880) and the build trial (CI run 45948159854). Not executed here: a real package publication, a real incident, and a restore after real data loss; the release decision still blocks the initial and extended releases while any required gate's evidence is stale.

rust/vater_core ports checked_add and the state-transition table (no dependencies, no unsafe code). Kani 0.68.0 with CBMC 6.11.0 verified, in the formal-rust CI job (run 46123196334), four harnesses comparing them with separately written specifications over their whole input range: every u64 pair and every u32 pair for the sum, every pair of the seven states, and all 49 pairs enumerated; every cover was satisfied (evidence/formal/kani-results.json). Kani runs only in that job, never in a Python job, and its result is recorded apart from the Python test results; CI requires each later run to reproduce the record.

The grant check (LocalAuthority.permits with the clock as an input) and the approval binding check of OperationLedger.begin_dispatch are ported to Rust and verified by Kani for every combination: every 64-bit tool and destination grant, revoked or not, any or no deadline, every clock value, publisher and request; every reservation and approval binding, use flag, expiry and ledger clock. Both harnesses verified with all covers satisfied in CI run 46123196334, recorded separately from the Python authorization tests, which check the same decisions on the shared literal rows.

docs/kani_assumptions.json lists each harness's input domain, its excluded inputs and each kani::assume with a written justification (one assumption: a state index below 7, which removes no state pair). Every harness has cover statements, and Kani reported all 14 satisfied, so no assumption empties a harness; Kani's own unsupported-construct checks on library panic paths all succeeded (unreachable). The test keeps the audit identical to the source and forbids stubs, expected panics, assume(false) and unsafe code.

tests/fixtures/independent_expected_values.txt holds 93 expected values written as literals from the documented policy (14 sums, all 49 transitions, 20 grant decisions, 10 approval cases), never computed from either implementation. The Python suite checks the real core and the real SQLite ledger against every row, and the Rust suite (cargo test in the formal-rust job) reads the same file, so both are compared on the same inputs. The values were written by the author from the specification, not by a person; human review of the fixture is the pull request review.

All 20 formal verification tasks are done with executed evidence; this report reruns every mapped case in one session (153 cases). The Lean results (evidence/formal/lean-4.19.0.log) and the Kani results (CI run 46123196334, evidence/formal/kani-results.json) are CI or recorded runs whose hashes and records are re-checked; Lean and Kani are not run by this report. What stays unproved is listed in docs/FORMAL_VERIFICATION.md (task.formal_verification.020).

src/verified_execution/webhooks.py accepts a delivery only with a valid HMAC-SHA256 signature of the raw body under a shared secret of at least 16 bytes, sent as sha256=<64 hex digits> and compared with hmac.compare_digest. Eight kinds of forged notification (no signature, another algorithm, the wrong secret, a tampered body, a truncated, upper-case, empty or non-hex digest) are refused with 401 before anything is parsed or stored.

Each delivery id is recorded once in the receiver's own SQLite file: a duplicate is acknowledged without being applied again, a reused id with another body is refused (409), and a resource's event that is not newer than the last applied one is recorded as stale. All six arrival orders of three events end in the newest state, and eight concurrent copies of one delivery apply it once (one BEGIN IMMEDIATE transaction).

Recording a delivery, applying it and marking it processed happen in one transaction. A delivery whose processing was interrupted (its result lost) stays received with no partial effect and is applied when redelivered; a resend of a processed delivery is acknowledged without effect. reconcile() compares the sender's delivery list with the log and names deliveries that never arrived and ones the sender failed to deliver, for redelivery; a missing delivery is never assumed not to have happened.

The released runtime executes no externally written code, so the WebAssembly runtime is not introduced into the release: pyproject.toml packages only verified_execution and verified_execution_contracts, requirements-py313.lock has no wasmtime, and no release module imports it. wasmtime 50.0.1 is only in the optional prototypes' lock; docs/optional/WEBASSEMBLY.md records the decision.

docs/optional/WEBASSEMBLY.md compares wasmtime, wasmer, wasm3 and Pyodide on compute, time and memory limits and Python access, and records why wasmtime 50.0.1 was chosen. Its threat model names, for every threat, the test that exercises the control; the test checks each named test exists.

A module may import only reviewed host functions that the run grants, with exactly the reviewed type; an unreviewed function, an ungranted one, an unknown grant or a mismatched type is refused before instantiation, so nothing outside the allowlist can be called.

The guest receives only its input. With a secret in the host environment, a guest that dumps its whole linear memory returns only zeros and its own input; an earlier run's input is absent because every run uses a fresh store.

No WASI is ever defined: modules importing path_open, fd_write, fd_read, sock_accept, sock_send, environ_get, clock_time_get or random_get are refused even when every host function is granted, so file, network, environment, clock and randomness access is denied by default.
Fuel bounds the instructions a guest executes: an endless loop ends with fuel_exhausted at exactly the configured fuel, without output, well within the time limit.
Store limits cap memory, tables and instances: a module declaring 100 pages is refused before it starts, and memory.grow and table.grow past the limit return -1 inside the guest.

An epoch deadline stops a guest at the time limit. A run stopped before any effectful host call ends as interrupted (nothing happened outside); a run stopped after an effectful call, or whose sink failed, ends as unknown, never as failed, and keeps the effects it delivered for reconciliation.

Each host function (vater.emit, effectful; vater.fail, no effect) has a recorded side effect and review, and each run's outcome lists exactly the host functions it was given: only those the module imports and the run grants.

The vater-wasm-abi/1 interface fixes the export types and the input and output data types; values of the wrong type, range or field set are refused before the guest runs, output of the wrong shape is a guest error, and a module with mismatched export types is refused.

Only modules whose SHA-256 the host approved are compiled: an altered, unlisted or extended module is refused without being compiled, and an approved digest of text-format source is refused as not a binary core module. The committed approval names exactly the fixture's binary.

Additional OS isolation is recorded as required before accepting third-party modules, because a wasmtime escape would reach the host process. run_isolated runs the same checks in a child process with an empty environment, no file writes (RLIMIT_FSIZE 0, observed EFBIG) and a CPU limit; a child that dies is interrupted or unknown, never finished. Network namespaces and seccomp are recorded as not covered.

Resource exhaustion (endless loop, memory and table bombs, deep recursion) and leak attempts (memory dumps, out-of-bounds output and emits) all end without any operation outside what was granted; repeated runs accumulate nothing.

scripts/measure_wasm_cost.py measured the same addition per call: Python core 0.136 microseconds, wasmtime in process (fresh store) 118 microseconds, behind the process boundary 69 milliseconds; compile 2.8 ms; wasmtime adds 30,232,307 installed bytes. docs/optional/WEBASSEMBLY.md compares security and cost from these numbers, with the Python core as the baseline.

Measured over real loopback HTTP against the local REST interface for 20 jobs: REST needs 20 requests for their states, 21 with the tool schema (7,527 bytes against GraphQL's 2,707), and cannot list jobs by state at all; GraphQL answers each in one request. No current consumer needs these queries, so GraphQL is not introduced into the release.

Queries over 4 KiB or 400 tokens, deeper than 5, with more than 15 aliases, lists over 50 items (literal or variable) or cost over 300 (counted through fragments) are refused before any resolver runs, as are invalid or cyclic ones; ordinary queries and introspection within the limits are answered.

The principal comes only from the host-issued credential; another principal's job reads exactly like a missing one by id, variable, alias, fragment, inline fragment and in lists, no schema field or argument names a principal, and a principal claimed in the request body is ignored over HTTP.

Every inter-process channel (stdio MCP, loopback HTTP, the shared SQLite ledger, test subprocess JSON lines) stays on one host, so gRPC is not introduced; neither lock holds gRPC or protobuf and no source imports grpc. The condition for reconsidering is recorded.

src/vater_optional/proto_compat.py defines the .proto version compatibility test: removing a field without reserving its number and name, changing its type or cardinality, renaming it, or reusing a reserved number or name is reported; adding new numbers is compatible; constructs it cannot judge are refused, not skipped.
MCP, local HTTP and the local line interface all call the same ToolRuntime on one host: there are not several independent executors, so no delegation target exists and Agent2Agent is not introduced.

src/vater_optional/delegation.py fixes delegation: explicit tool subsets only, a positive budget held back from the parent, expiry within the parent's and one hour, bounded re-delegation, and no approval travelling with a delegation (only the root human principal approves). Wildcards, unbounded budgets and expiries are refused.

The target editors are decided (Claude Code and Visual Studio Code, as MCP clients of the stdio server); the official conformance run passes tools-list, tools-call-simple-text and tools-call-error, so no further editor protocol is investigated or implemented.

Measured in Chrome for Testing 158.0.8127.36: document.modelContext (not navigator.modelContext) exists only with the experimental web platform flag; the page names insecure_context, no_model_context and unsupported_api, and docs/optional/WEBMCP.md records the observed API and that WebMCP is a Community Group draft. Run in Chromium 158 (Playwright 1.63.0), where document.modelContext exists only with --enable-experimental-web-platform-features.

Only add_numbers runs in the page and it makes no request; checked_add and send_report, which need the core or an external effect, go to the Python host. Run in Chromium 158 (Playwright 1.63.0), where document.modelContext exists only with --enable-experimental-web-platform-features.

The page registers its three tools through registerTool; the browser lists them with the page's origin, input schemas and annotations (readOnlyHint, consequentialHint) and executes them through executeTool. Run in Chromium 158 (Playwright 1.63.0), where document.modelContext exists only with --enable-experimental-web-platform-features.

The browser does not check inputSchema, so the page checks types, ranges, lengths, required and unexpected fields itself; ten kinds of invalid agent arguments are refused before anything reaches the host. Run in Chromium 158 (Playwright 1.63.0), where document.modelContext exists only with --enable-experimental-web-platform-features.

The page principal may call only its two-tool grant through an HttpOnly, SameSite=Strict session; claimed principal, authority or approval fields are ignored, and requests without the session, from another origin or without an Origin are refused. Run in Chromium 158 (Playwright 1.63.0), where document.modelContext exists only with --enable-experimental-web-platform-features.

Host operations are decided again in Python: a request that skipped the page's checks is refused by the common core (INVALID_ARGUMENT, OVERFLOW) and a valid one runs through its authorization states. Run in Chromium 158 (Playwright 1.63.0), where document.modelContext exists only with --enable-experimental-web-platform-features.

The activity list labels each execution as the user (a trusted click) or an AI agent (a WebMCP call); a script-made click is not shown as the user. Run in Chromium 158 (Playwright 1.63.0), where document.modelContext exists only with --enable-experimental-web-platform-features.

send_report runs only after an operator approves that exact request with the operator credential; the page session cannot approve, instructions placed in the page change nothing, changed arguments need a new approval, and an approval is used once. Run in Chromium 158 (Playwright 1.63.0), where document.modelContext exists only with --enable-experimental-web-platform-features.

Without WebMCP the page says why and works as an ordinary page: both additions and the report submission (up to approval) run by clicks. Run in Chromium 158 (Playwright 1.63.0), where document.modelContext exists only with --enable-experimental-web-platform-features.

The Content-Security-Policy blocks the third-party and inline scripts; code assumed to run anyway cannot read the session, reach the page's internals or replace a tool, and the host refuses it other tools and approval. Run in Chromium 158 (Playwright 1.63.0), where document.modelContext exists only with --enable-experimental-web-platform-features.

Five configurations (headless shell and new headless, with and without the flag, and an insecure origin) are recorded with their results in evidence/optional/webmcp-compatibility.json and reproduced by a fresh run; the adopted browser is Chromium 158 with the flag, and Firefox, WebKit and Edge are recorded as not tested here. Run in Chromium 158 (Playwright 1.63.0), where document.modelContext exists only with --enable-experimental-web-platform-features.

Promotion to a required entry needs measured demand (20% of users over 30 days), at least two engines without flags, the safety tests passing in each browser with zero bypasses in an external penetration test, and a fixed specification; the current measurements do not meet them.

The chosen computation is square float32 matrix multiplication (1 <= n <= 512), checked on a hand-computed case. Run on Chromium 158's SwiftShader adapter (a software GPU; there is no hardware GPU here or in CI), so correctness and the checks are executed, while speed figures describe SwiftShader.
The Python CPU reference fixes inputs (seeded, float32), output (float32) and precision (the exact sum rounded once), checked against exact rational arithmetic.
The reference's time and tracemalloc peak are recorded for n = 32, 64 and 128 (9.8 ms / 42,907 bytes to 229.3 ms / 664,724 bytes).
Only public or synthetic data may go to the GPU; internal, confidential and personal data and unknown labels are refused before leaving the host.

The WGSL shader declares two read-only array<f32> inputs, a read_write array<f32> output and a u32 size uniform, and compiles and runs. Run on Chromium 158's SwiftShader adapter (a software GPU; there is no hardware GPU here or in CI), so correctness and the checks are executed, while speed figures describe SwiftShader.

Invalid sizes, lengths, non-finite values and non-Float32Array inputs are refused by the page and the host before any buffer; sizes that are not multiples of the workgroup give exact results with the shader's bounds check. Run on Chromium 158's SwiftShader adapter (a software GPU; there is no hardware GPU here or in CI), so correctness and the checks are executed, while speed figures describe SwiftShader.

The tolerance is the float32 accumulation bound n * 2^-24 * sum|a_ik b_kj| + 2^-24 |exact|; sequential float32 sums stay inside it and a value twice the bound away is caught. Run on Chromium 158's SwiftShader adapter (a software GPU; there is no hardware GPU here or in CI), so correctness and the checks are executed, while speed figures describe SwiftShader.

GPU results for exact and general float32 inputs (n = 13, 16, 48, 64) agree with the CPU reference within the tolerance and are accepted by the host. Run on Chromium 158's SwiftShader adapter (a software GPU; there is no hardware GPU here or in CI), so correctness and the checks are executed, while speed figures describe SwiftShader.

The GPU round trip including buffer creation, upload, dispatch and readback is measured next to the JavaScript and Python CPU paths (n = 128: 7.1 ms against 7 ms in JavaScript): the total time did not improve over the fastest CPU path on the software adapter. Run on Chromium 158's SwiftShader adapter (a software GPU; there is no hardware GPU here or in CI), so correctness and the checks are executed, while speed figures describe SwiftShader.

A lost device is replaced at most once and then computed on the CPU: losing every device stops after two requests, losing only the first recovers on the GPU. Run on Chromium 158's SwiftShader adapter (a software GPU; there is no hardware GPU here or in CI), so correctness and the checks are executed, while speed figures describe SwiftShader.

docs/optional/WEBGPU.md records that the GPU is not a security boundary and that isolation and authorization stay with the Python host's common core; the host refuses short, non-finite, out-of-tolerance and malformed GPU results.

Adoption follows from the measurements: WebGPU stays only on a hardware adapter with a round trip at least twice as fast as the fastest CPU path at every size and every result within tolerance. Applied to the recorded numbers the rule says not adopted (software adapter, no speedup).

All 14 WebAssembly isolation tasks are done with executed evidence; this report reruns every mapped case in one session (35 cases) with wasmtime 50.0.1 from requirements-optional-py313.lock. The prototype (src/vater_optional/wasm_sandbox.py) is not part of the release; docs/optional/WEBASSEMBLY.md records that the release does not introduce it and that OS isolation beyond the measured child process (network namespaces, seccomp) is not covered.

All 12 additional protocol tasks are done with executed evidence; this report reruns every mapped case in one session (91 cases). GraphQL, gRPC, Agent2Agent and further editor protocols are not introduced into the release; the GraphQL, .proto compatibility and delegation prototypes live in src/vater_optional, with the conditions for reconsidering each in docs/optional/MORE_PROTOCOLS.md.

All 12 WebMCP tasks are done with executed evidence; this report reruns every mapped case in one session (21 cases) in Chromium 158 (Playwright 1.63.0), where document.modelContext exists only behind --enable-experimental-web-platform-features. Firefox, WebKit and Edge were not tested; the promotion conditions in docs/optional/WEBMCP.md are not met, so WebMCP stays an optional entry.

All 12 WebGPU tasks are done with executed evidence; this report reruns every mapped case in one session (30 cases) on Chromium 158's SwiftShader adapter. There is no hardware GPU here or in CI: correctness, validation, device loss and the host's checks were executed, while the speed figures describe a software adapter, and by the recorded rule WebGPU is not adopted.
